Carlson: USGS data release, 2002–2022, 361 fires in 26 states, 1,770,939 building points, 73,534 destroyed; binary destroyed/not from analysts' visual interpretation of pre/post imagery; protocol covers major buildings only. No update cadence is stated. DINS: CAL FIRE Damage Inspection, California only, 2013-08 to 2025-11 in our archive, 445 incidents, 132,522 structures; field inspection with No damage / Affected / Minor / Major / Destroyed (plus Inaccessible). Publication lag not measured; newest record 2025-11-23 as of Sept 2026. We train on the Carlson fires from the Sentinel-2 era (191 fires, 2016–2022) and 8 DINS incidents (2024–25).

Key

Destroyed

All inspected records

Carlson

Calls every major building out to 2.4 km: 294,209 direct, 1,476,730 indirect. 98.4% of its destroyed are within 100 m.

CAL FIRE

Inspects the burned area and its edge: no records beyond about 1 km. 99.2% of destroyed are inside the perimeter.

Our record

Uses Carlson's frame: 84% of our rows are indirect. Indirect calls are hard to check: Carlson's own indirect F1 is 0.12.

15 CAL FIRE fires 2024–25, 38,497 records, final WFIGS perimeters · zones are distances, not how a building caught fire · diagram not to scale

Carlson's frame (and ours): the fire perimeter plus 2.4 km; Direct = inside or within 100 m, Indirect = 100 m to 2.4 km, the 'ember buffer'. CAL FIRE inspects damaged and threatened structures: across 15 forward fires, 73% of its records are inside the perimeter, 23% within 100 m outside it (mostly undamaged buildings; median 51 m out), and none beyond 2.4 km; 0 of 17,902 destroyed records fall outside our frame. So CAL FIRE gives us truth for the direct zone only. The owner's hypothesis is largely right, with two caveats: 'direct/indirect' is a distance label, not an observed ignition mechanism, and CAL FIRE does list many undamaged buildings just outside the perimeter. Consequences: on Eaton the indirect ring holds 59% of rows but only 5 destroyed calls, and the model scores F1 0.00 on the 527 inspected structures there; scoring only direct rows raises our Carlson mean per-fire F1 from 0.780 to 0.797.

Current public release v0.12.0: 653 fires · 35 states · 2002–2026 · 2.26 M building rows · 100,074 destroyed · every building scored by the final models

Carlson and DINS become the training truth for a model that reads public satellite imagery, so the record keeps going where they stop. Release v0.12.0 (published 28 September 2026): 653 fires in 35 states, 2002–2026, 2,258,471 building rows and 100,074 destroyed (73,534 from the USGS census carried verbatim, 26,540 called by our models). 292 fires are past 2022 (32 states, 347,522 buildings, 17,684 destroyed) and 469 are outside California (34 states, 580,559 buildings, 25,568 destroyed). Every building our models score is scored by the final first call model with its neural column; 62 fires also carry the second call. 66,265 Microsoft-footprint rows are withheld from the public file for licence reasons. 'All structures' is the direction set on 23 September: every footprint, every damage type, labelled by uncertainty tier; damage grades are in testing.

Two ways to average: per fire and pooled

Every score in this deck is one or the other. We lead with per fire.

Three fires, three scores (illustration)

0.95

Big fire

1,000 buildings

0.80

Medium fire

100 buildings

0.50

Small fire

10 buildings

The 10 largest of the 191 Carlson fires hold 45% of all buildings (Woolsey alone 9%), so the pooled score mostly reflects a handful of giant fires. A 20-building fire matters to its community as much as Woolsey does to its own.

per fire

Per fire

Score each fire on its own, then average the fires. Every fire counts the same.

(0.95 + 0.80 + 0.50) ÷ 3 = 0.75

Answers the product's question: how good is the call for a fire? Our ❶ first call: 0.80.

pooled

Pooled

Put every building from every fire in one pile and score the pile once. Big fires dominate.

≈ 0.93

Mostly says how we do on the few biggest fires. Our ❶ first call: 0.90.

Key

Per fire: the headline in every chart

Pooled: shown quieter, for reference

Illustrative numbers on the left · real ❶ first call, Carlson fires: 0.80 per fire, 0.90 pooled · F1 at the 0.88 cut, each fire held out

Per-fire F1 is the mean of each fire's own F1 (fires with at least one destroyed building); pooled F1 is computed once over every building. Pooled is dominated by the largest fires: the ten biggest of 191 Carlson fires hold 44.6% of buildings (Woolsey 8.8%). The product reports fire by fire, so per-fire F1 is the headline and pooled is kept as a secondary reference, drawn outlined and lighter throughout the deck.

Step zero: the Structure Inventory Model

Both models only score buildings on this list. A house missing here is missing from the loss count, so the list is fixed from imagery taken before ignition.

Start

Footprint databases

FEMA USA Structures and Microsoft footprints, kept only if drawn from imagery dated before the fire.

Fill the gaps

Roof detector

A neural network reads 0.6 m aerial photos and adds roofs the footprint databases missed.

Output

Tagged inventory

One point per building, tagged by source and size (major ≥ 50 m²). Possible phantom footprints are kept, not deleted.

0.81

of major buildings are in our inventory (0.77 with footprints alone)

0.83

of our points are real USGS buildings

1 in 11

footprints, at most, with no USGS building nearby

Scored on held-out blocks of 5 California fires (2017–18), major buildings, match within 10 m · the public release omits Microsoft footprints (licence)

Before either call, every fire needs a list of the buildings that stood there. Footprints: FEMA USA Structures polygons kept if their IMAGE_DATE is before ignition; Microsoft v2 polygons kept if their capture window ends before the fire (undated ones are kept too; the Microsoft 2022 release is admitted as a whole for fires after its release date). Detector: a U-Net (ResNet-34 encoder, checkpoint the production detector) on 4-band 0.6 m NAIP with the footprints as a fifth band, trained on 43,364 chips from 39 areas; the probability map is cut at 0.5, patches of at least 20 m² become points, and any point inside a footprint buffered by 3 m is dropped. Numbers: on held-out blocks of 5 California fires (Creek, Thomas, Tubbs 2017; Camp, Woolsey 2018; 38,821 census buildings) recall is 0.768 with footprints alone and 0.809 with the detector, precision 0.832. On 17 California fires the recall ranges 0.59 to 0.91 (median 0.77) and precision 0.83 to 0.96. Phantom footprints (no census building within 10 m): 0.148 raw, 0.094 for major-sized footprints in core areas; both are upper bounds. A multi-year NAIP union exists but is used only in validation, and the triage score is not in the release.

8 / 50

How we build the structure inventory

Five steps, shown on one real place: rural lots in the Park Fire (2024), on the pre-fire aerial photo.

1

Start from footprint maps

USA Structures (FEMA/ORNL) and Microsoft outlines drawn before the fire.

2

Look for roofs ourselves

A neural network (U-Net) reads the 0.6 m pre-fire photo, with the known footprints as a hint, and scores every pixel for 'roof'.

3

Group roof pixels

Roof pixels are joined into patches; patches under 20 m² are dropped.

4

Add only what's new

A patch becomes a new building point only if it lies outside every known footprint (3 m margin).

5

One point per building

The inventory = footprint points plus the new points. Every damage call is made on these.

0.82

of Carlson's buildings are in our inventory (36 fires)

0.89

of our inventory points are real buildings

What it misses: Weakest on small sheds, buildings under trees, and destroyed homes on older fires whose footprints were drawn after the fire.

Area shown: about 145 m × 82 m, USDA NAIP July 2022 · diamonds = new points from our model · rings = CAL FIRE inspections, coloured by grade

Structure Inventory Model settings: the production detector, a ResNet-34 U-Net on NAIP RGB + NIR plus a footprint prior band; roof threshold 0.5; 8-connected patches of at least 20 m²; a patch becomes a point only if it lies outside every USA Structures or Microsoft footprint buffered by 3 m. Inventory = footprint points (pre-fire) + new points. Against Carlson on 36 fires: 0.82 of Carlson's buildings are in the inventory and 0.89 of inventory points are real buildings.

Key

Destroyed buildings in our inventory

Surviving buildings in our inventory

On older fires, destroyed homes are often missing from footprint databases drawn after the fire. A missed building never gets a damage call: on 17 California fires our destroyed count is 0.77 of Carlson's.

Share in our inventory = recall: matched to a CAL FIRE or Carlson building within 20 m (types) or 10 m (destroyed vs surviving) · small, low buildings are hardest

Recall by CAL FIRE structure type on 15 forward fires from 2024–25 (38,497 inspected structures; one-to-one match within 20 m, from the pipeline's own match table; pooled 0.786). Motor homes and trailers are small, move, and are often under cover, so almost none are in footprint databases or visible to the detector. Outbuildings are small and often under trees. Destroyed vs surviving: on the held-out blocks of the 2017–18 Carlson fires, 0.627 of destroyed and 0.848 of surviving major buildings are found (footprints alone: 0.521 vs 0.821), because USA Structures snapshots postdate those fires: 74 percent of 2017's destroyed structures have no footprint at all. On 2024–25 CAL FIRE fires the gap nearly closes (0.773 vs 0.798). End to end on 17 California fires we recover 6,451 of Carlson's 10,808 destroyed buildings and add 1,862 destroyed calls Carlson did not record as destroyed.

Precision has been measured only in California (0.83–0.96 on 17 fires) and at Marshall, CO (0.93) · density = inventory points within 100 m · tree cover from pre-fire greenness (NDVI)

Outside California we can only measure recall, against Red Cross and FEMA damage assessments (within 10 m, shipped inventory). In California, 17 fires give recall 0.59 to 0.91 and precision 0.83 to 0.96 (pooled 0.77 and 0.88); by EPA region: Mediterranean California 0.78 / 0.88, Northwestern Forested Mountains 0.74 / 0.88, Marine West Coast Forest 0.81 / 0.88 (recall / precision). Six of those 17 fires trained the detector and score a little higher. The one non-California fire with both a census and our inventory, Marshall CO 2021, scores recall 0.967 and precision 0.929 (suburban, an easy case). Density: rural buildings with few neighbours are the most often missed (0.565). Tree cover is a proxy from pre-fire Sentinel-2 greenness (NDVI) at 30 m: within-fire quarters from barest to greenest, and dense canopy = NDVI at least 0.65.

Structure Inventory Model run on Carlson fires with Carlson's own frame (MTBS perimeter + 2.4 km), matched one-to-one within 10 m to Carlson's major buildings, precision in the 100 m core. Batch 1: 20 stratified fires in all 18 states and 9 EPA Level I regions plus 17 California fires: 36 fires, 182,925 Carlson buildings. Recall 0.817, precision 0.894 (California 0.811 / 0.894; outside 0.852 / 0.899). Destroyed 0.681 vs surviving 0.827 — the main weakness, same inside and outside California. By source: USA Structures points 0.905 precise and find 67% of buildings; Microsoft 0.970 precise, 11% (28% outside California); detector 0.668 precise, +4.7 recall points. Public release without Microsoft rows: recall 0.716 (0.574 outside California); putting back detector points dropped as Microsoft duplicates recovers 0.735–0.739. Canopy: about 0.85 in sparse canopy, 0.58 at NDVI ≥ 0.6. Size: 0.77 under 100 m², 0.80–0.88 for 100–400 m², 0.69 at 400 m² and up. End to end (found and called destroyed by the first call): 0.622 overall, 0.626 California, 0.589 outside; 0.541 for the public release. One-fire regions (Tropical Wet Forests, Northern Forests) are single fires and noisy.

Surviving buildings: better every year

Newer fires sit closer to when the footprint maps were drawn, so more of what stood is on the map: 0.79 → 0.83 → 0.85.

Destroyed buildings: worst on recent fires

The maps were mostly drawn after these fires. A house lost in 2021 was a bare lot when it was mapped; one lost in 2015 may have been rebuilt, and the rebuild is in our inventory.

What to expect in 2026

A 2026 fire happens after the maps were drawn, so destroyed buildings were still standing when mapped. We expect them to be in our inventory about as often as surviving ones (≈ 0.85). The DINS test below checks this directly.

In progress: the forward check on CAL FIRE fires, 2017–2025. The same inventory run on every CAL FIRE inspection fire, on pre-fire 0.6 m aerial photos, to show how recall changes as fires approach 2026.

First 36 Carlson fires (batch 1 of 191) · match within 10 m, major buildings · fire years 2014–2022 · full run and CAL FIRE check in progress

Recall of Carlson buildings by the full Structure Inventory Model (USA Structures ∪ Microsoft ∪ detector) on batch 1 (36 fires, 18 states), by fire year. Surviving: 0.789 (2014–17, 8 fires, 42,086 buildings), 0.834 (2018–20, 13 fires, 86,978), 0.852 (2021–22, 15 fires, 41,438). Destroyed: 0.681 (2,243), 0.703 (7,040), 0.631 (3,140). Public release without Microsoft: surviving 0.725 / 0.731 / 0.714, destroyed 0.638 / 0.603 / 0.518. Missed overall 21.6% / 17.6% / 16.4%. Interpretation: footprint databases were largely digitised from post-fire imagery; destroyed recall on old fires is propped up by rebuilding. For a prospective fire the footprints predate the fire, so the destroyed/surviving gap should close; the 2017–2025 CAL FIRE inventory run tests this.

14 / 50

Two different models, two calls on every building

Separate models with different inputs. The first answers fast; the second waits a year for more evidence and makes a more certain call.

First call model

74 days after ignition

  • Sentinel-2 before vs after the fire
  • Neighbourhood and fire context
  • Same season a year earlier

+ neural column

Second call model

About a year after

  • Sentinel-2 before vs after the fire
  • Satellite embeddings, year before vs after
  • A full year of change over time

+ neural column

Both ship side by side as separate columns; the second call does not overwrite the first.

These are two separately trained models, not one model run twice. First call model (the production first call model, in production since v0.11.0): 235 tabular inputs plus the 74-day neural column, available about ten weeks after ignition. Second call model (the production second call model): the base Sentinel-2 signals plus the AlphaEarth embedding pair, a year of per-scene dynamics, a second post-fire window and the one-year neural column; it needs a year of imagery and embeddings exist only from 2017, so it covers fewer fires. Both use the same 0.88 threshold. The neural column (blue throughout) is a separate network whose output is added to each model as one more input.

The network's reading of the whole image history, as one more signal

235 signals + the neural column → gradient-boosted trees → probability · called destroyed at 0.88 or above

Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance from Microsoft Planetary Computer. Bands: blue, green, red, near-infrared, shortwave infrared 1 and 2. Indices: NBR (normalized burn ratio), NDVI (vegetation), NBR2 (char and ash), NDWI (moisture). Before = median of clear pre-fire scenes; after = median of clear scenes 14 to 74 days after ignition; each at the building's own pixel and the mean of its 3 x 3 pixel block, plus before-after differences: 62 base signals. Families: (F) neighbourhood percentile ranks, 48 signals: each building's change ranked against its 50 nearest buildings and against its whole fire; (C) 1 km fire context, 63 signals: how burned the surrounding area is, plus the EPA ecoregion; (S) same-season pre-window, 62 signals: a composite from the same season one year before, which removes seasonal vegetation change. Together they added +0.0265 mean F1 per fire. The model is HistGradientBoosting (scikit-learn).

Read left to right like a tournament bracket. Top bracket: Sentinel-2's six bands (blue, green, red, near-infrared, two shortwave infrared) are combined into four burn indices (NBR, NDVI, NBR2, NDWI); bands and indices are measured before and after the fire, at the building's own pixel and averaged over its 30 m block, giving 62 base signals. Middle bracket: three families of context, 173 signals: the building's change ranked against its 50 nearest neighbours and its fire (48), how burned the surrounding kilometre is plus the ecoregion (63), and the same measurements from the same season a year earlier (62). Bottom bracket: the neural network reads every clear scene and adds one probability. All 236 inputs go to a gradient-boosted tree model (scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting), which outputs a probability; 0.88 or above is called destroyed.

Second call model: a year of evidence

A separately trained model. It starts from the same base signals, then adds what only time can show.

Satellite embeddings

A yearly 64-number summary of every 10 m pixel. The year before vs the year after the fire.

A year of change

Every clear look out to 12 months: does the site recover, stay bare, or get rebuilt?

A second after-image

A later post-fire window, after smoke and ash have cleared.

Trade-off: it waits a year, and embeddings start in 2017, so it covers fewer fires.

Plus a neural column: the one-year network's probability, as one more signal.

Production second call model since v0.11.0 · called destroyed at 0.88 or above

Embeddings: Google DeepMind AlphaEarth Foundations annual satellite embeddings, a 64-dimension vector per 10 m pixel per year, available from 2017. We use a clean pre-fire year and the first post-fire year. Dynamics: per-scene change features out to +365 days. Second window: a later post-fire composite. The one-year neural column adds +0.102 per fire [+0.087, +0.119] over the base signals. This is the production second call model since v0.11.0: Carlson 0.925 pooled / 0.828 per fire, CAL FIRE 0.969 / 0.933.

Its inputs: the same 62 Sentinel-2 base signals; Google DeepMind's AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings (a yearly 64-number summary of every 10 m pixel) for a clean pre-fire year and the first post-fire year; per-scene change features from every clear look out to 365 days (does the site recover, stay bare, or get cleared and rebuilt?); a later post-fire composite; and the one-year neural column. Production model the production second call model: Carlson 0.925 pooled / 0.828 per fire, CAL FIRE 0.969 / 0.933; +0.102 per fire over the base signals.

The neural network reads the whole image history

Every clear scene

Dozens of Sentinel-2 looks per building, before and after

One token per look

bands, burn indices, change vs its own pre-fire self, date

Transformer + CNN

over time, plus the image patch around the building

One new column

its probability joins the tree model's table

Trained honestly

Each fire's column comes from a network that never saw that fire

Augmented

Random brightness and timing shifts teach it to ignore haze and revisit gaps

Time-legal

For the ❶ first call it sees only the first 74 days of the fire it scores

Tested and dropped: bigger networks, pooling, recurrent encoders, label-noise losses, sun-angle inputs

Tokens are 12 reflectance channels (the building's own pixel and its 3x3 mean) plus six indices and their difference from the building's own pre-fire mean; up to 128 time slots with a sinusoidal date encoding. A small transformer reads the sequence; a small CNN reads the 3x3 patch (wider 5x5 and 7x7 patches are being tested on the full imagery). Stacking: the network outputs one probability per building, joined as a column into the gradient-boosted tree, which learns how much to trust it. Leave-one-fire-out end to end. Augmentation that won: radiometric jitter plus time jitter, without rotations (+0.0059 over with rotations, canonical). Headline: +0.076 per fire [+0.062, +0.091] for the full first call model over the 62-signal base. Both networks are saved and score every fire in the record. A net trained on randomly truncated histories (all horizons) was tested and gives no gain at 74 days (+0.002, interval spans zero); an earlier screen figure (+0.0325) was a caching error and is withdrawn.

819,000 buildings · 73,000 destroyed

Testing

Leave one fire out. Every fire is scored by a model that never saw it, 199 times over.

Two scores. Pooled F1 counts every building; per-fire F1 counts every fire equally.

Four seeds, averaged, with intervals from resampling whole fires.

Carlson training fires start in 2016 because that is when Sentinel-2 imagery begins

Pool: 818,838 buildings, 73,443 destroyed. Carlson fires before 2016 predate Sentinel-2, so they are not in the training pool; they remain in the published record verbatim. F1 balances false alarms and misses. Per-fire F1 is the primary metric (a fire with 20 destroyed homes counts as much as Camp); pooled F1 is reported beside it. Fires with fewer than 100 buildings or 10 destroyed are reported but excluded from the per-fire average (188 of 191 Carlson fires qualify). Intervals come from resampling whole fires, never individual buildings, because buildings in one fire are not independent.

How a new input earns a place

three steps, in order

1

Pre-register

Write down the test and its pass mark before any model is fitted.

2

On its own, the new input must add at least +0.005 F1 per fire, with a 95% interval above zero.

3

Promote

Refitted with everything else: at least +0.005 over production and no state worse than −0.010. CAL FIRE is reported, not a gate.

Guards on every run

rules that keep the scores honest

Leave one fire out

Every score comes from a model that never saw that fire, including the neural columns.

Folds checked

The code refuses to run if training and scoring share a building or a fire.

No location, no fire facts

No latitude, longitude, fire size or perimeter distance as inputs.

Time-legal

The ❶ first call only sees imagery up to 74 days after ignition, checked every run.

Leakage probes

Before any F1 is read, probes test whether inputs can rebuild location or the label.

Sealed 2026 test

Models, cut and windows were locked on 10 Sep; 2026 fires are kept for one final read.

Inclusion policy of 17 Sep 2026, CAL FIRE gate dropped 29 Sep · details in the experiment ledger

Inclusion rule: admission, the family alone adds at least +0.005 mean per-fire F1 on Carlson-191 with a paired fire-level 95% interval excluding zero; promotion, the joint refit adds at least +0.005 over production with no state (3+ fires) worse than −0.010. The CAL FIRE-8 'not worse' gate was dropped by the owner on 29 Sep 2026; CAL FIRE is still reported separately. The +0.005 bar is a post-hoc relaxation of an original +0.010, flagged in the ledger. Leakage guards: leave-one-fire-out; neural columns from 5-fold GroupKFold by fire with disjointness checks; no lat/lon or fire characteristics; first-call imagery +14 to +74 days; label-missingness and location probes; the sealed 2026 freeze.

25 / 50

F1: one score for misses and false alarms

Precision

Of the buildings we call destroyed, the share that really were. Low precision means false alarms.

Recall

Of the buildings really destroyed, the share we caught. Low recall means misses.

F1

A balance of the two. It is high only when both are high; 1.0 is perfect.

Worked example

90 caught

10 missed

5 false alarms

Precision 0.95

Recall 0.90

F1

0.92

Why not accuracy? Only about 7% of buildings are destroyed, so a model that calls every building "survived" is 93% accurate, yet its F1 is zero.

Every F1 in this deck: the destroyed call at 0.88, each fire held out. Scores are averaged per fire unless a slide says pooled.

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2 x P x R / (P + R), which equals 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN). Harmonic rather than ordinary mean, so a model cannot hide weak recall behind strong precision or the reverse. Worked example: TP 90, FP 5, FN 10 gives precision 0.947, recall 0.900, F1 = 180 / 195 = 0.923. True negatives (surviving buildings correctly called survived) do not enter F1 at all, which is why it suits a rare outcome like destruction; accuracy is dominated by them. The calls depend on the threshold: a building is called destroyed when its probability is 0.88 or above, and moving that cut trades precision against recall. Pooled F1 counts every building in one pile; per-fire F1 computes F1 for each fire and averages, so a small fire counts as much as Camp. AUC, shown later, is threshold-free.

The label ceiling: how it is calculated

A perfect model is still marked wrong wherever the label is wrong. The ceiling is the best F1 it can get against Carlson's labels.

1

Where both teams graded

43,929 buildings on 14 California fires carry a Carlson label and a CAL FIRE label. They disagree on 2.1%.

28,608

both: destroyed

663

only CAL FIRE: destroyed

280

only Carlson: destroyed

14,378

both: standing

2

Estimate each team's error rate

A Hui–Walter latent-class model (1980) treats the true status as unknown. Splitting the fires into two groups with very different loss rates gives six equations for six unknowns, so each team's error rate can be solved for without assuming either team is right.

finds losses

clears survivors

CAL FIRE

99.5%

98.4%

Carlson

98.6%

99.0%

3

Score a perfect model

Simulate a model that always knows the truth, then grade it against Carlson's labels with those error rates, at our own share of destroyed buildings (about 7%). Its F1 is the ceiling.

0.934

all buildings

0.853

per fire

95% range from resampling the 14 fires 2,000 times: 0.88–0.97 all buildings, 0.79–0.93 per fire. Our ❶ first call (0.80 per fire) is already inside that range.

Holds up

Splitting by era gives the same error rates. Outside California the two teams disagree just as often (2.0% vs 2.1%) and the same way; Marshall, CO, with a third grader, agrees.

Weak spots: it is an upper bound

If the two teams' mistakes are linked (both miss the same sheds), the ceiling drops: to 0.90 / 0.80 at a 0.3 correlation. Error rates also vary fire to fire, and outbuildings are much noisier (ceiling 0.87 vs 0.94 for houses).

How to pin it down

A third, blind grader on about 950 buildings that both teams call standing, in high-loss fires. The current review sample (all high-score, Carlson-standing) cannot do it.

Hui & Walter (1980) latent-class model, two strata (8 fires ≥ 50% destroyed, 6 below) · ceiling by simulation at Carlson-191 prevalence

Two-stratum Hui–Walter on 43,929 dual-labelled buildings (14 CA fires, 2017–2022). High-loss stratum 31,488 buildings (apparent prevalence 0.82), low-loss 12,441 (0.28). Unique admissible root, residual 0: CAL FIRE Se 0.9951 / Sp 0.9835; Carlson Se 0.9855 / Sp 0.9904. Era split agrees to ≤ 0.002; leave-one-fire-out jackknife keeps Carlson Se in [0.963, 0.990] (Camp is the lever). Ceilings (Carlson labels): pooled F1 0.9338 at π = 0.0711 (bootstrap 0.884–0.970); mean per fire on the 188 Carlson fires 0.853 (0.786–0.927). 91% of the ceiling loss comes from survivors labelled destroyed (ρ₋), which is why the per-fire ceiling is low: on a fire with few losses, a handful of false 'destroyed' labels cut F1 sharply. Robustness (29 Sep): constant Se/Sp across fires is rejected (G² 928 on 24 df); per-fire strata give 0.924 / 0.836; dependence is unidentified by two raters and lowers the ceiling (ρ 0.2: 0.915 / 0.822; ρ 0.3: 0.901 / 0.802), so the published value is an upper bound. Outbuildings: Carlson Se 0.965, ceiling 0.868. Outside CA disagreement 2.0% (5,003 buildings); Marshall CO three-rater fit Carlson Se 0.991 / Sp 0.979. docs/label-ceiling-robustness-2026-09-29.md.

The lean-DINS rule: how it works and what the evidence says

The rule

When Carlson says survived and CAL FIRE's inspector says destroyed, the building counts as destroyed. Recorded 29 Sep 2026.

How it is applied

A side-car corrections file: 633 buildings flipped (matched within 10 m), 16 held back where CAL FIRE matches disagree. The original label file is never edited.

Both truths reported

Every evaluation reports the original and the corrected truth side by side.

Our models side with CAL FIRE on these cases

All ruled pairs

62%

Single-family homes

70%

Matches within 3 m

70%

Outbuildings

54%

Manual review agrees

Checking the imagery: 74% of single-family disagreements are Carlson errors; mobile homes 20 of 22.

But: small effect

Scoring against the corrected truth adds +0.002; retraining with it changes nothing measurable (−0.002 per fire, interval spans zero).

Recommendation: adopt the corrections at the next retrain and always report both truths · the models also side with CAL FIRE 65% of the time in the reverse direction, so this is partly model agreement, not proof

Owner ruling recorded in docs/experiment-ledger.md (29 Sep 2026). Side-car lean_dins/corrections_v1.csv flips 633 points (632 in the training pool) where Carlson = surviving and a CAL FIRE DINS match within 10 m = destroyed; 16 held back because their DINS matches disagree; the reverse direction (DINS surviving, Carlson destroyed) is not flipped. Evidence: out-of-fold probabilities side with DINS on 62% of the ruled pairs (about 70% for single-family homes and for matches within 3 m; 54% for outbuildings); in the reverse direction they side with DINS about 65% too, so agreement partly reflects the model learning CAL FIRE's standard. QA verdicts: 74% of single-family disagreements are genuine Carlson errors; mobile homes 20 of 22. Effect: +0.002 pooled when scoring against corrected truth; retrain with corrected labels −0.002 per fire (2 seeds / 1 seed).

AUC: how well the model ranks, before any cut

Pick one destroyed and one surviving building at random. AUC is the chance the model scores the destroyed one higher.

0.5 is a coin flip; 1.0 is perfect ordering. F1 also depends on where the 0.88 cut falls; AUC does not.

ModelCarlson, allCarlson, per fireCAL FIRE, all
❶ First call model0.9940.9790.991
❷ Second call model0.9960.9830.995

High AUC, low F1 means the ranking is right but the cut is wrong. That is the pattern on Plains grass fires, where a region-aware threshold is the next fix.

Area under the ROC curve · leave-one-fire-out · four-seed mean probability · per fire = mean over 188 Carlson fires

← called standing

0.88 cut

destroyed →

0 · surely standing

0.5

1 · surely destroyed

AUC = area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; it measures ordering only, across every possible threshold. Both final models rank destroyed above surviving buildings about 99.5 percent of the time. The remaining F1 errors are mostly about where scores fall relative to the fixed 0.88 cut, not about ordering. External Plains fires (Oklahoma 2025 grass fires) showed high AUC with low recall under an earlier model, which is why a region- or prevalence-aware threshold is the next improvement. The AUC ceiling implied by label noise is about 0.988, which we exceed; the F1 ceiling is therefore conservative. The strip under the table is an illustration, not data: each house sits at its predicted probability of destruction, coloured from green (0) to red (1); the dashed line is the 0.88 cut, so everything to its right is called destroyed. AUC asks only whether destroyed houses sit to the right of surviving ones; F1 also depends on where the dashed line falls.

Familiar ground vs a region never seen

Carlson fires, F1 per fire. Two tests on the same fires; only the training set changes.

Test 1: hold out one fire

Train on every other fire, including the rest of its region. Score the one left out; repeat for every fire.

Test 2: hold out the whole region

Train only on other regions, so the landscape is new to the model. Score all of the region's fires.

On 1–9 fires the ranking stays good (AUC 0.97–0.98) but recall drops to 0.74–0.77. 13 of 77 incidents score zero and 32 score a perfect 1: with a median of 8 inspected buildings, one miss swings the score.

Tuning the cut

Chosen honestly (on other fires only), a lower cut for fires the model counts as small gains +0.10 per fire on the inspected buildings (+0.14 ❷ second call).

…but not on real fires

On 17 small fires scored in full, 0.88 already over-counts (69 called vs 57 destroyed); lower cuts add false alarms the inspections cannot show.

What does help

Training on small incidents: the retrained ❷ second call gains +0.062 per fire on this tier with no change of cut. Report small fires as low-count estimates, typically within ±2 buildings.

Carlson has only one such fire (Logan, CO: 6 destroyed) · new incidents scored by a model that never saw them

Tiers: Carlson has 1 fire with 1–9 destroyed (Logan CO 2017: 111 rows, 6 destroyed), 125 with 10–100 and 65 over 100; the 8 CAL FIRE training incidents are all 10+; the new 2023–25 CAL FIRE incidents add 77 fires with 1–9 destroyed (median 8 inspected buildings). Per-fire F1 here has no floor (every fire has at least one destroyed building). CAL FIRE per fire with 1–9: 0.735 (first), 0.742 (second); without: 0.882 and 0.876; alone: 0.701 and 0.711; count error about 0.8 buildings per fire. Threshold rules, chosen leave-one-fire-out: a count-based cut (model's own count at 0.88, bins 0 / 1–2 / 3–9 / 10+) gains +0.100 [+0.035, +0.169] first call and +0.140 [+0.064, +0.225] second call on the inspected rows, about zero on larger fires. On 17 incidents matched to full v0.12.0 inventories, 0.88 predicts 69 destroyed vs 57 true; the count-based rule 87, a 0.5 cut 108: worse. Recommendation: keep 0.88, report small fires as low-count estimates (typical error ±2), train on small incidents (second call v2: +0.062 [+0.005, +0.126] on this tier), and build a full-inventory truth panel for all 77 small incidents before judging any small-fire rule.

Recommended: calls at 74 d, 365 d and about 730 d once a two-year model passes a held-out test · no continuous updating: trough months would flip calls

Per-scene separability of destroyed vs surviving buildings (mean per-fire AUC of the change from each building's own pre-fire baseline), in time bins from −365 to +731 days, Carlson fires. It peaks at +30 to +44 days (NBR 0.91), falls through a trough at +150 to +250 days (regrowth, snow, cleanup), partly recovers near a year (red rises as lots stay bare or are rebuilt), and troughs again at +450 to +635 days. Widening windows: pre −60, −120, −180 d and second-call post +100, +150 d are all flat (intervals span zero; 20 grouped folds, 2 seeds). The first call's post window cannot exceed +74 d by design. A third call near +730 d gained +0.029 on an earlier horizon curve, not yet a production fit.

What is missing, and how we flag it

Buildings we can't see

Footprint databases find 74% of inspected structures; the detector adds 3.5% of the rest. On 2017–18 fires destroyed homes are missed more often (34% vs 21%). Microsoft rows withheld: 66,265.

Imagery gaps

642 buildings have no damage call at all (incomplete imagery). 11% have 3 or fewer clear looks; 34% on 2016 fires (one satellite). Nothing before 2016.

No ❷ second call yet

206,119 rows: not applied to the unit (106,280), recent fires awaiting the 2026 embeddings (62,425), fires before 2017 (36,658), other (756).

Gaps in the answer key

Carlson has no structure type. CAL FIRE covers only the direct zone. Outside California, recall can be checked but precision cannot.

Missing is never filled in

Every gap is flagged in the release: damage_null_reason, refined_null_reason, detector_outcome, pre_n_obs / post_n_obs, raster_n_cells. Zero and missing are different; nothing is imputed.

Counts from the v0.12.0 manifest and the inventory audits · details and recovery options per gap in the speaker notes

Inventory: footprint-database recall against CAL FIRE is 0.744 at 10 m; the detector adds 343 structures (3.5% of 9,845 missed). USA Structures alone finds 48.5% of later-destroyed buildings but 82.2% of survivors on the older fires; with the detector, 70.4% of destroyed. Undated Microsoft footprints: CA 5%, CO 30%, UT 35%, WA 40%. 2024–25 fires use 2022 NAIP, so newer buildings are missed. Imagery: 642 rows have no first call (reason incomplete_optical_features). Second call: 281,413 rows have one over 62 fires; 206,119 do not, each with a reason. Labels: 60.8% of Carlson's destroyed buildings have no typed present-day footprint; South Fork is the only verified non-California truth set after 2022 and supports recall only.

v0.12.0 · cloud, shadow and snow masks from Sentinel-2's scene classification · 2 buildings failed both windows

642 refusals re-counted from the release. Cause: the cloud/shadow/snow mask covered the building's own pixel in every scene of the pre-fire window (447 rows) or the post-fire window (193; 2 failed both). No scene was missing and tile edges were not the cause. CZU 2020: 348 (coastal fog); Deep Woods, Black Cove and Fish Hook, North Carolina 2025: 186 (spring cloud); Waterfall Mountain VA: 25; Otter Creek KS: 22; Clayton 2016: 18 (too few early-archive scenes). Recoverable: 640 of 642 from cached scenes by widening the pre window to −60 days (or the seasonal pre-fire composite) and the post window to +200 days; this changes model inputs, so it needs a flag column and a leave-one-fire-out check before shipping.

Proposed production model: where it makes calls

Keep the current models, trained on every fire. Apply three rules before a fire is scored, so calls are only made where the models are reliable.

R1 · Where we call

Calls only in the six western regions. The Great Plains and the East are out of domain: they behave alike on every test.

R2 · What we call

Significant structures: 50 m² or more (major). Outbuildings, sheds, motor homes and trailers are listed but not called.

R3 · How we report

Fire-level scores only where the model counts 25 or more destroyed. Smaller fires are called and reported by count.

What it costs in v0.12.0

Fires out of domain

33.7%

Destroyed buildings out of domain

11.1%

Minor structures not called

+1.1% of buildings

In-domain fires with a fire-level score

111 of 157

Rules use region, footprint size and the model's own destroyed count, never the true loss · retraining on in-domain fires only made the models slightly worse, so training keeps every fire

Applicability rules, not model inputs. R1: no calls in EPA Level I region 9 (Great Plains); regions 5, 8 and 15 (east) get a low-confidence flag because the training pool has only 8 fires there; the six western regions 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 13 are in-domain. R2: in the product, structure_class = major (pre-fire footprint at least 50 m²); for CAL FIRE evaluation, every type except utility/misc, motor home, travel trailer and infrastructure (mobile homes stay in); Carlson is major-only already. R3: fire-level metrics only for fires with at least 10 destroyed, using the ICS-209 count or else the model's own count (right side of 10 for 276 of 286 fires). Coverage in v0.12.0: the region rule removes 24.7% of fires, 8.3% of structures and 7.1% of destroyed; minor structures another 1.1% of structures; fires under 10 destroyed are 34.8% of fires but 0.5% of destroyed. Among the fires our models scored, 71% have fewer than 10 destroyed. The Plains rule also drops good fires such as Marshall 2021 and the Colorado Front Range suburbs. Retraining on in-domain fires only: first call −0.0043 per fire [−0.0064, −0.0024], so the Plains fires help the West.

Second call: Carlson 0.8282 → 0.8446, CAL FIRE 0.9327 → 0.9716. Selection bias: the Great Plains was chosen in about 90% of random halves (100% using the strict region-out scores); out-of-sample per-fire gain +0.015 vs +0.019 in-sample, so bias-checked per-fire F1 is 0.818 (first) and 0.842 (second). Strict held-out penalties in-domain (first call, Carlson): region −0.035, state −0.034, year −0.018; a new in-domain fire should be expected to score about 0.785 per fire. Limitations: truth is 191 Carlson fires and 8 CAL FIRE incidents, all CAL FIRE in California; the footprint-size proxy for R2 recovers only part of the CAL FIRE gain in the product; calls in the East rest on 8 fires; the second call has no strict panel; the ceiling is a lower bound.

48 / 50

Five lessons from what we tested

New information beats bigger models

The neural column (+0.076, +0.102) and cheap extra channels drove the gains. Every architecture change and extra detector band was a null.

Every headline needs its control

Four results were reversed by a cache or a join bug: distillation, the +0.0325 horizon result, the 'does not travel' verdicts, a detector cache.

Time matters, for a model that reads a sequence

The trees peak at 74 days; the network keeps gaining for a year. About 63% of the ❷ second call's lead is extra time.

Judge on the population the product scores

Small-fire and adaptive cuts look good on inspected rows and fail on full inventories. The fixed 0.88 stands.

Labels are near their ceiling

Where Carlson and CAL FIRE disagree the model is at chance, so relabelling, pseudo-labels and noise-aware losses were null.

Using Microsoft's building footprints (2.85% of release rows) means the whole database must be published under ODbL. That is the only limiting factor.

What ODbL is

An open licence for databases: from Open Data Commons.

Anyone may use it: copy, use, adapt and build on the data, including commercially.

Credit required: users must credit the source.

Share-alike for the database: an adapted version of the database must also be ODbL; maps and results made from it can be licensed however their makers like.

Our code stays MIT.

Decision of 29 September 2026 · counts from the v0.12.0 release and the inventory check on 36 Carlson fires

Owner decision 29 Sep 2026: the release is licensed ODbL 1.0 so the Microsoft-derived rows (66,265 rows, 2.85% of v0.12.0; 28% of found buildings outside California) can be included. All other sources are public domain, CC BY or open and need only credit. Code remains MIT.
